newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia govt says will help states with tax loss.
newsitem.headline: Australia govt says will help states with tax loss.

text.p: Australian Treasurer Peter Costello said on Tuesday the national government would help states make up lost revenue after a landmark court ruling outlawed state levies on tobacco, alcohol and petrol worth billions of dollars.
"If the states request assistance in relation to revenue the Commonwealth (national government) will certainly seek to accommodate them," Costello told reporters.

In a four to three majority ruling earlier on Tuesday, the High Court of Australia ruled that state business franchise fees were in fact an excise, which only the national government can raise under Australia's constitution.

Constitutional experts said the federal government would have to swiftly levy its own taxes to replace the state charges, which account for about 16 percent of the income raised by Australia's six states and two territories.
Costello said federal assistance was conditional on prices remaining steady and that the money raised by Canberra for the states be publicly acknowledged as a state tax.
"If the Commonwealth is asked to assist in any collection in order to try and give certainty to state revenue and revenue base, the Commonwealth would see fit to do so," Costello said.
It was not immediately clear how consumers could be shielded from price rises.
The current fees vary across states and one, Queensland, has no levy at all on petrol. But the consitition bans Canberra from setting different rates in different states.
Australia's most populous state, New South Wales, said it would ask the national government to top up state revenue to make up for the income lost through Tuesday's judgment.
State premier Bob Carr, calling the ruling a constitutional crisis, said it would cost his state A$1.8 billion a year.
The states and territories already rely on Canberra for about half their income, divided up at a traditionally acrimonious annual summit of state, territory and national leaders.
